slides.say: b and y are integers. Given: y is equal to b minus three, squared, plus b plus eight, cubed. Which of the following statements is necessarily true?
So all the choices are about even and odd. [short pause] We'll solve it three ways, with the two brackets, dropping the powers, and then plugging in numbers.
[short pause] Let's start with the two brackets. Both are built from the same b. From b minus three up to b plus eight is a jump of eleven, an odd jump.
And an odd jump always switches between even and odd. From two, a jump of eleven lands on thirteen, and from five, on sixteen. So one bracket is even, and the other is odd.
A power doesn't change parity, so after the powers, still one even and one odd. Odd plus even is odd. So y is always odd. Choice number four is our answer.
at: Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Another way, and it's the shortest. It uses the same rule, powers don't change parity, but instead of thinking about the brackets, we just drop the powers. In a parity question that's allowed, and I'd never do that in a regular equation.
at: never do that in a regular equation

slides.say: Without the powers, b minus three plus b plus eight is two b plus five. Two b is always even, whatever b is, and even plus five is odd. So y is always odd. Choice number four.
at: So y is always odd. Choice number four

slides.say: [pause] Now let's try plugging in. It's easier to choose b than y. b is one. One minus three is negative two, and squared is four. One plus eight is nine, and nine cubed is seven twenty-nine. Four plus seven twenty-nine is seven thirty-three, odd.
b is two. Two minus three is negative one, and squared is one. Two plus eight is ten, and ten cubed is a thousand. One plus a thousand is a thousand one, odd again.
So b can be odd or even, and choice numbers one and three are out. y was odd both times, so choice number two is out. Choice number four. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: b can be odd or even
